title: The asymptotic spectrum of tensors is connected
problem: Strassen's theory of asymptotic spectra describes when many copies of one tensor can be converted into many copies of another, which governs the matrix multiplication exponent, the asymptotic rank conjecture, cap-set bounds and the asymptotic conversion of multipartite entangled states. The duality says such a conversion is possible exactly when every spectral point, a monotone homomorphism to the nonnegative reals, takes a smaller value on the source. Little is known about the shape of the set of spectral points. Strassen asked whether, for a fixed tensor, their values form an interval.
result: For every order \(k\ge3\), the asymptotic spectrum of complex \(k\)-tensors is contractible, and in particular path-connected: every spectral point is joined by a continuous path to each flattening rank. Consequently, for every complex tensor \(s\), the values of the spectral points at \(s\) fill the closed interval from its asymptotic subrank to its asymptotic rank, answering Strassen's question. The method also re-proves Strassen's log-star-convexity for rectangular matrix multiplication, extends it to polynomial multiplication tensors, and proves that the non-crossing upper quantum functionals are spectral points on all complex tensors.
significance: Connectedness turns Strassen's duality into polynomial inequalities on one interval, so for a tensor \(t\) and polynomials \(p,q\) with nonnegative integer coefficients, \(p(t)\) asymptotically restricts to \(q(t)\) exactly when \(p\le q\) on that interval. This opens a route to bounds on asymptotic rank, including possibly on the matrix multiplication exponent, from conversions whose difference is not monotone, which all previous upper bounds on \(\omega\) avoided. The quantum functionals, which measure asymptotic conversion of multipartite pure states under local operations, gain a self-contained proof.
limitations: The result describes the topology of the spectrum, not its points: it does not construct new spectral points beyond interpolations of known ones, and it does not by itself improve any bound on \(\omega\) or on asymptotic rank. Path-connectedness is proved over the complex numbers; over other fields only log-star-convexity for matrix multiplication and graph tensors is shown. The authors state that the research ideas are theirs and that Claude, ChatGPT and gpt-6-astra were used to work out proof details and check proofs.

description: A \(k\)-tensor \(s\) restricts to \(t\) if local linear maps on each leg turn \(t\) into \(s\). Spectral points are functions \(f\) that are additive under direct sum, multiplicative under the Kronecker product, monotone under restriction, and normalized by \(f(\langle1\rangle)=1\). Strassen's duality theorem states that \(s^{\otimes n}\) restricts to \(t^{\otimes(n+o(n))}\) if and only if \(f(s)\le f(t)\) for every spectral point; the asymptotic rank of \(t\) is the largest spectral value at \(t\), and the asymptotic subrank the smallest. In quantum information, restriction is conversion of multipartite pure states by stochastic local operations, so the same spectrum governs asymptotic entanglement transformations.

The known spectral points include the flattening ranks, Strassen's support functionals and the quantum functionals of Christandl, Vrana and Zuiddam, defined through moment polytopes and marginal entropies. If these were all the points for 3-tensors, then \(\omega=2\). The structure of the whole set was largely unknown; connectedness had been proved only on special families of tensors or along special families of points.

Why it matters is visible already for matrix multiplication. Schönhage's \(\tau\)-theorem bounds \(\omega\) from a conversion of a sum of matrix multiplication tensors into a unit tensor, because the difference \(r-\sum_ih_i^\sigma\) decreases in \(\sigma\). For a sum on both sides, \(\sum_j\ell_j^\sigma-\sum_ih_i^\sigma\) need not be monotone. Strassen showed that the spectrum on \(\langle2,2,2\rangle\) is the interval \([4,2^\omega]\), so a negative value of the difference at any \(\sigma>2\) bounds \(\omega\). The new theorem gives the same interval principle for every complex tensor.

The proof is an abstract interpolation theorem. For two spectral points \(f_0,f_1\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), the weighted geometric mean \(f_0^{1-t}f_1^t\) is not a spectral point in general, because it fails additivity. It becomes one when restricted to a well-chosen multiplicatively closed class \(\mathcal A\) of building blocks, into which powers of every tensor decompose with subexponentially many pieces, provided a cover property holds. For complex tensors, \(\mathcal A\) comes from decomposing tensor powers into isotypic components of the symmetric group, a method-of-types construction, together with subspace averaging.

methods.technique: Interpolating spectral points through a decomposable class
methods.explanation: Given two spectral points, one wants a continuous family between them. The geometric mean is multiplicative and monotone but not additive; the fix is to define it only on blocks where additivity is not needed and extend it by taking the best block inside high powers.
math: Call \(a_1,\ldots,a_q\in\mathcal A\) an \(\mathcal A\)-decomposition of \(s\) if each \(a_j\le s\) and \(s\le a_1+\cdots+a_q\). If powers \(s^n\) have such decompositions of length \(2^{o(n)}\), every spectral point satisfies \(\max_jf(a_j)\le f(s)^n\le q\max_jf(a_j)\), and taking \(n\)-th roots shows that a spectral point is determined by its values on \(\mathcal A\). Define \[F_t(s)=\sup\Bigl\{\bigl(f_0(a)^{1-t}f_1(a)^t\bigr)^{1/n}:\ n\ge1,\ a\in\mathcal A,\ a\le s^n\Bigr\}.\]

Theorem 1.3 shows that \(t\mapsto F_t\) is a path in the spectrum from \(f_0\) to \(f_1\), with \(F_t(a)=f_0(a)^{1-t}f_1(a)^t\) on blocks, whenever \(f_0,f_1\) have the cover property: if \(a^n\le s_0+s_1\), then \(f_0(s_0)/f_0(a)^n+f_1(s_1)/f_1(a)^n\ge2^{-o(n)}\). The key step expands \((a_1+\cdots+a_q)^n\) and assigns each term to whichever of \(f_0,f_1\) gives it the smaller relative value. If the cover property holds for every \(f_0\) against a fixed \(f_1\), such as a flattening rank, the map \((f_0,t)\mapsto F_t\) is jointly continuous, and the spectrum is contractible.
methods.transfer: The theorem is stated for abstract Strassen semirings, so it applies to other asymptotic problems with a duality theorem, for example the Shannon capacity of graphs, where the paper gives illustrations, and asymptotic conversions in resource theories with a semiring structure.

methods.technique: Connectedness as a test for asymptotic restrictions
methods.explanation: Duality turns an asymptotic restriction into infinitely many inequalities, one per spectral point, and unknown spectral points make them hard to use. If the values at a tensor form an interval whose endpoints include a known point, a single sign change of a polynomial is enough to conclude.
math: For a polynomial \(p(x)=\sum_ic_ix^i\) with nonnegative integer coefficients, set \(p(t)=\bigoplus_i\langle c_i\rangle\otimes t^{\otimes i}\); every spectral point satisfies \(f(p(t))=p(f(t))\). Corollary 1.2 states \[p(t)\lesssim q(t)\iff p(x)\le q(x)\ \text{for all }x\in[\underset{\sim}{Q}(t),\underset{\sim}{R}(t)],\] where \(\underset{\sim}{Q}(t)\) and \(\underset{\sim}{R}(t)\) are the asymptotic subrank and asymptotic rank. So if \(p(t)\lesssim q(t)\) is known and \(p(x)>q(x)\) at some \(x\) above a flattening rank of \(t\), then the asymptotic rank of \(t\) is below \(x\), even if \(p\le q\) again for larger \(x\).

Editorial illustration from Fig. 2: the conversion behind \(\omega\le9/4\) gives the monotone difference \((2a-1)^{18}-a^{8\sigma}\), whose zero \((9/4)\log(2a-1)/\log a\) is \(2.88\) at \(a=10\), \(2.42\) at \(a=10^4\) and \(2.29\) at \(a=10^{16}\), tending to \(9/4\). A non-monotone difference could cross zero earlier and then recover; only connectedness lets that early crossing count.
methods.transfer: The interval criterion applies to any problem phrased as asymptotic conversion of powers of one tensor, including rates of converting copies of a multipartite state into GHZ states, where the asymptotic subrank plays the role of the GHZ extraction rate.
